title: Play in the style of John Petrucci
goal: Play in the style of John Petrucci

steps.title: Alternate picking precision
steps.description:
[Before you start]
Advanced roadmap: already play power chords with rests, one minor-scale position, basic hammer-ons/pull-offs and a whole-tone bend; identify root, third and fifth. Check eight bars of eighth-note rhythm at 90 BPM before starting. Use a six-string guitar, metronome and recorder. Keep a short riff and a melodic phrase alongside the technical drills from the beginning. Work on a specific problem in short blocks, then apply it to that music. Existing session and resource completions remain valid; revised checks are for self-assessment, not a requirement to repeat completed steps.

[What it is]
Alternate picking alternates downstrokes and upstrokes.

[Why it matters]
Establish an even pulse before adding crossings; this is the foundation for articulated runs.

[How to practice]
On the B string play frets 5-7-8-7 as sixteenth notes, one bar playing then one bar resting. Start slowly; repeat starting on an upstroke. Let the pick clear the string without forcing one wrist position.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
Martin Goulding, John Petrucci: Prime Numbers (educator-authored study): https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/john-petrucci-prime-numbers
steps.successCriteria: Record four play/rest cycles at 70 BPM for each starting stroke; all four notes remain distinct and the first note of each beat meets the click. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Economy picking transitions
steps.description:
[What it is]
Economy picking carries a stroke across adjacent strings when the phrase permits it.

[Why it matters]
Treat it as an articulation choice alongside alternate picking, not a requirement for every Petrucci run.

[How to practice]
Use G-string 5-7-9 followed by B-string 5-7-8, ascending D-U-D-D-U-D. Reverse with U-D-U-U-D-U. Compare with strict alternate picking at the same tempo.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, A Clean Sweep: https://www.guitarworld.com/features/clean-sweep-mastering-sweep-arpeggios-john-petrucci
steps.successCriteria: Record eight ascending and eight descending six-note groups as eighth-note triplets at 60 BPM; crossings have no extra accent or pause. Explain which strokes cross in the same direction. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Cross-string picking control
steps.description:
[What it is]
Cross-string control applies the picking pulse to adjacent strings.

[Why it matters]
Isolating a crossing exposes timing errors hidden in a long scale run.

[How to practice]
Alternate pick G-string 5-7-9 and B-string 5-7-8 up and down as eighth-note triplets. Isolate the last note of one string and first of the next, then restore the group; try both starting strokes.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
Martin Goulding, John Petrucci: Prime Numbers (educator-authored study): https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/john-petrucci-prime-numbers
steps.successCriteria: Record eight bars at 70 BPM with each starting stroke; no skipped note, accidental third string or delay at a crossing. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Pick angle consistency
steps.description:
[What it is]
Pick angle consistency means repeatable contact, not freezing the hand at one angle.

[Why it matters]
A useful angle lets the pick clear the strings while retaining the intended attack.

[How to practice]
Play eight bars of eighth notes on B-string fret 7 at 80 BPM. Compare two comfortable amounts of edge contact, then use the quieter-scraping choice on a two-string pattern. Film the picking hand without forcing a posture.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
Martin Goulding, John Petrucci: Prime Numbers (educator-authored study): https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/john-petrucci-prime-numbers
steps.successCriteria: Record both comparisons and eight bars of crossings at 80 BPM; choose a contact that does not catch the string and explain the audible difference. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: String attack dynamics
steps.description:
[What it is]
Attack dynamics gives identical notes different weight.

[Why it matters]
It supports both singing leads and the accented, muted rhythm side of this style.

[How to practice]
Play E5 eighth notes: two bars soft, two medium, two accented, then two bars with accents on beats 1 and 3. Compare clean and lightly distorted sounds while keeping the pulse and palm-mute depth stable.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
Jamie Hunt, Petrucci rhythm style (original teaching studies, not Dream Theater transcriptions): https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/dream-theater-john-petrucci-rhythm-style
steps.successCriteria: Record the eight-bar sequence at 90 BPM; the three levels and planned accents remain audible without rushing the louder notes. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Synchronization pick-left
steps.description:
[What it is]
Hand synchronization means the fret is ready when the pick sounds the note.

[Why it matters]
This step diagnoses the coordination behind the earlier picking patterns rather than adding a new speed target.

[How to practice]
Play B-string 5-6-7-8 as sixteenths with one bar of rest after each bar. Record slowly and locate doubled attacks or buzz; loop only the faulty pair before rebuilding the four-note group.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, Practice Tips, Part 1: https://www.guitarworld.com/blogs/john-petrucci-practice-tips-part-1
steps.successCriteria: Record four play/rest cycles at 70 BPM and name the transition you corrected; no buzz or separated fret/pick attack is audible. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Tremolo picking control
steps.description:
[What it is]
Tremolo picking repeats a pitch with measured strokes.

[Why it matters]
Petrucci describes mandolin-like tremolo in The Oddfather; the goal here is controlled repetition, not maximum endurance.

[How to practice]
On one comfortable fretted note alternate one beat of sixteenths with one beat of rest. Build to one bar playing and one resting; accent the first note of each beat and finish with a sustained note.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci interviewed by Jon Wiederhorn, Terminal Velocity track by track: https://www.guitarworld.com/features/john-petrucci-details-terminal-velocity-track-by-track-these-songs-had-to-have-a-message-and-the-best-way-to-do-that-is-through-melody
steps.successCriteria: Record four bar-length play/rest cycles at 90 BPM, with four strokes per beat, clean stops and an intentional sustained ending. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Legato strength and clarity
steps.description:
[What it is]
Legato joins hammer-ons and pull-offs into one timed phrase.

[Why it matters]
The later sweep and tapping combinations depend on these notes remaining audible without extra picking.

[How to practice]
On the B string play 5-7-8-7 as sixteenths, picking only the first note of each group. Work in one-bar bursts followed by rest. Use only enough fretting force to sound the note; avoid squeezing for volume.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, Descending E Mixolydian Run: https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/betcha-cant-play-john-petruccis-descending-e-mixolydian-run
steps.successCriteria: Record four play/rest cycles at 60 BPM; all four notes are audible, evenly spaced and free of adjacent-string noise. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Hammer-on power control
steps.description:
[What it is]
Hammer-on control produces a deliberate second note without another pick stroke.

[Why it matters]
Focus on timing and sufficient contact rather than hitting as hard as possible.

[How to practice]
On B-string 5-7, then 5-8, pick the lower note and hammer the upper as eighth notes. Alternate two bars softer and two bars louder, keeping the lower finger comfortable.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, Descending E Mixolydian Run: https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/betcha-cant-play-john-petruccis-descending-e-mixolydian-run
steps.successCriteria: Record eight bars at 70 BPM covering both intervals and both dynamics; upper notes speak on time without pulling sharp or adding a pick attack. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Pull-off articulation
steps.description:
[What it is]
Pull-off articulation keeps descending notes audible.

[Why it matters]
A controlled release is essential to the descending picked-and-legato vocabulary demonstrated by Petrucci.

[How to practice]
On B-string 8-7-5, prepare the lower fingers, pick 8 and pull off twice as eighth-note triplets. Use a small release that sounds the next note without catching the high E string.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, Descending E Mixolydian Run: https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/betcha-cant-play-john-petruccis-descending-e-mixolydian-run
steps.successCriteria: Record eight bars at 60 BPM; all triplet notes speak, the final note does not arrive early and the adjacent string stays silent. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Wide-interval legato
steps.description:
[What it is]
Wide-interval legato connects more distant pitches with an appropriate fingering.

[Why it matters]
Reach is not the objective: a position shift or slide can preserve the phrase more comfortably than a held stretch.

[How to practice]
On the high E string compare 12-15 with 12-17 using a slide for the wider connection if needed. Play an eighth-note pair then a quarter-note rest. The linked stretch exercise is preparation only, not this musical task.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, Descending E Mixolydian Run: https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/betcha-cant-play-john-petruccis-descending-e-mixolydian-run
John Petrucci, Practice Tips, Part 1: https://www.guitarworld.com/blogs/john-petrucci-practice-tips-part-1
steps.successCriteria: Record eight comfortable pairs at 60 BPM with each chosen fingering; land on the intended pitch on time and explain where you shifted instead of holding a stretch. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Left-hand finger independence
steps.description:
[What it is]
Finger independence is controlled note choice and release, not making every unused finger motionless.

[Why it matters]
It supports reliable changes of fingering in legato and picked lines.

[How to practice]
On B-string frets 9-12 play 9-11-10-12, then 12-10-11-9 as eighth notes. Release unnecessary pressure between notes; compare with the linked coordination exercise.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, Practice Tips, Part 1: https://www.guitarworld.com/blogs/john-petrucci-practice-tips-part-1
steps.successCriteria: Record eight bars at 70 BPM, alternating the patterns; every intended note sounds once with no unwanted sustained note. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Left-hand muting precision
steps.description:
[What it is]
Fretting-hand muting silences unused higher strings and released notes; the picking hand can damp lower strings.

[Why it matters]
Their combined role becomes especially audible under distortion.

[How to practice]
Play a four-note fragment across G and B, then a full beat of silence. Identify which hand stops each unused string. Repeat clean and with moderate gain, including a position shift.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, A Clean Sweep: https://www.guitarworld.com/features/clean-sweep-mastering-sweep-arpeggios-john-petrucci
steps.successCriteria: Record eight bars at 70 BPM in both sounds; intended notes sustain until their release and all planned pauses are silent. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Finger stretch conditioning
steps.description:
[What it is]
Comfortable finger reach prepares wider fingerings without treating anatomical span as an achievement.

[Why it matters]
This remains a preparation step, not a demand to force a larger stretch.

[How to practice]
Use the linked four-fret pattern around frets 10-13 at a slow tempo. Release between notes and move the whole hand when useful. Compare a lower position only if comfortable; stop if playing hurts.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, Practice Tips, Part 1: https://www.guitarworld.com/blogs/john-petrucci-practice-tips-part-1
steps.successCriteria: Record two clean passes at 50 BPM in a comfortable position and demonstrate an alternative shifted fingering for a reach that feels cramped. Increasing span is not required. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Sweep picking accuracy
steps.description:
[What it is]
Sweep accuracy coordinates one directional picking motion with releasing each preceding note.

[Why it matters]
Learn a small triad before trying a continuous multi-string cascade.

[How to practice]
Use an A minor triad on G14-B13-e12, then reverse. Start with separate hand motions and join them as eighth-note triplets; release each previous note instead of holding a chord.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, A Clean Sweep: https://www.guitarworld.com/features/clean-sweep-mastering-sweep-arpeggios-john-petrucci
steps.successCriteria: Record eight bars at 60 BPM, ascending and descending; each pitch is separate, reversals stay in time and no chord rings across the sweep. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Arpeggio fingering fluency
steps.description:
[What it is]
Arpeggio fingering fluency connects chord identity to a playable shape.

[Why it matters]
Naming the notes prevents sweep shapes from becoming disconnected from the harmony.

[How to practice]
Find A-C-E and C-E-G on the top three strings in one position and another position. Pick them separately as eighth notes before using a sweep; resolve each pattern to its root.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, Using Triad Arpeggios to Imply More Complex Chord Qualities: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/wild-stringdom-john-petrucci-using-triad-arpeggios-imply-more-complex-chord-qualities
steps.successCriteria: Record each of the four shapes twice at 60 BPM, name their chord tones and land on the intended root without searching. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Sweep-to-legato integration
steps.description:
[What it is]
Sweep-to-legato integration changes articulation within one phrase.

[Why it matters]
It applies the previous two techniques; no extra pick attack is needed on a marked hammer-on.

[How to practice]
Sweep G14-B13-e12, hammer high-e15, then reverse through e12-B13-G14 as comfortable. Write the seven events, play them as eighth notes and rest for the eighth eighth-note slot.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, A Clean Sweep: https://www.guitarworld.com/features/clean-sweep-mastering-sweep-arpeggios-john-petrucci
John Petrucci, Descending E Mixolydian Run: https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/betcha-cant-play-john-petruccis-descending-e-mixolydian-run
steps.successCriteria: Record eight bars at 60 BPM; the marked hammer-on has no pick attack, every event occupies its written slot and the final rest is clean. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Multi-note string arpeggios
steps.description:
[What it is]
Multi-note string arpeggios place two chord tones on one string before moving onward.

[Why it matters]
Those same-string notes need legato or separate strokes; one sweep cannot articulate them all.

[How to practice]
Play an A minor shape G9-G14-B13-e12 as eighth notes and reverse it. Mark the shift on G and choose separate strokes or a slide there; reserve sweeping for adjacent-string moves.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, Using Triad Arpeggios to Imply More Complex Chord Qualities: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/wild-stringdom-john-petrucci-using-triad-arpeggios-imply-more-complex-chord-qualities
John Petrucci, A Clean Sweep: https://www.guitarworld.com/features/clean-sweep-mastering-sweep-arpeggios-john-petrucci
steps.successCriteria: Record eight bars at 60 BPM; name E-A-C-E, articulate both G-string notes and keep the shift inside the pulse. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: String crossing cleanliness
steps.description:
[What it is]
String crossing cleanliness checks the release side of an arpeggio.

[Why it matters]
It complements the earlier picking step by testing whether preceding strings keep ringing.

[How to practice]
Play the three-string triad from Sweep picking accuracy once with deliberate chord overlap, then once releasing each note. Repeat the separated version with moderate gain and a one-beat rest.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, A Clean Sweep: https://www.guitarworld.com/features/clean-sweep-mastering-sweep-arpeggios-john-petrucci
steps.successCriteria: Record eight separated phrases at 60 BPM in eighth-note triplets; explain the contrast and leave no preceding string sounding through the final rest. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Diminished arpeggio fluency
steps.description:
[What it is]
A diminished seventh arpeggio contains root, minor third, diminished fifth and diminished seventh.

[Why it matters]
Here it is a short tension-and-resolution tool, not a requirement to master every diminished pattern.

[How to practice]
Use B-D-F-Ab, then resolve to A-C-E over E7-Am. Play each pitch separately before choosing a fingering. The linked scale tool is support only; use these written chord tones for the task.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, Using Triad Arpeggios to Imply More Complex Chord Qualities: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/wild-stringdom-john-petrucci-using-triad-arpeggios-imply-more-complex-chord-qualities
steps.successCriteria: Record four two-bar phrases at 60 BPM in eighth notes; name the four diminished tones and resolve Ab upward to A at the chord change. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Augmented arpeggio control
steps.description:
[What it is]
An augmented triad has a root, major third and augmented fifth.

[Why it matters]
Compare it with a major triad so the altered tone has an audible purpose instead of becoming another speed shape.

[How to practice]
Play C-E-G, C-E-G# and A-C-E separately as quarter notes, resting on beat 4 of each bar. Then choose a comfortable three-string fingering; the linked sweep is only mechanical preparation.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.
This is an original application exercise. The source supports the broader harmony, articulation or meter approach; it does not attribute this exact example to Petrucci.

[Sources]

steps.successCriteria: Record four cycles at 60 BPM; identify G changing to G# and resolving to A, with no unintended notes ringing through the rests. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: String skipping accuracy
steps.description:
[What it is]
String skipping accuracy targets nonadjacent strings while keeping the unused string silent.

[Why it matters]
Start with a single gap before expanding the pattern.

[How to practice]
Alternate G-string 9 and high-e12 as eighth notes; mute B. Add G12 and high-e15 to make a four-note pattern, using strict alternate picking at a comfortable tempo.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
Martin Goulding, John Petrucci: Prime Numbers (educator-authored study): https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/john-petrucci-prime-numbers
steps.successCriteria: Record eight bars at 70 BPM; no B-string attack, missed target or delay occurs at a skip. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Two-handed tapping fluency
steps.description:
[What it is]
Two-handed tapping adds a picked-hand finger to a legato phrase.

[Why it matters]
The fretting-hand hammer and pull-off remain responsible for the lower notes.

[How to practice]
On high E play tap12-pull5-hammer8 as eighth-note triplets. First practise 5-8 alone, then add the tap; mute other strings and plan how to hold the pick.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, Descending E Mixolydian Run: https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/betcha-cant-play-john-petruccis-descending-e-mixolydian-run
steps.successCriteria: Record eight bars at 60 BPM; three even notes per beat, no extra open string and a clean return to one picked ending note. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Tapped arpeggio integration
steps.description:
[What it is]
Tapped arpeggios extend a chord shape to a higher chord tone.

[Why it matters]
Chord recognition comes before adding tapping speed.

[How to practice]
On high E use tap12-pull5-hammer8 for A-C-E, then tap15-pull8-hammer12 for C-E-G. Play one bar per chord as eighth-note triplets and mute unused strings.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, Using Triad Arpeggios to Imply More Complex Chord Qualities: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/wild-stringdom-john-petrucci-using-triad-arpeggios-imply-more-complex-chord-qualities
John Petrucci, Descending E Mixolydian Run: https://www.guitarworld.com/lessons/betcha-cant-play-john-petruccis-descending-e-mixolydian-run
steps.successCriteria: Record eight bars at 60 BPM with correctly timed changes; name both triads and make all three notes audible. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Wide-interval leaps
steps.description:
[What it is]
Wide-interval leaps create a contrast in register.

[Why it matters]
Hear the target pitch first so a large movement serves a melodic idea.

[How to practice]
Over Am alternate A on G14 with E on high-e12, then A on high-e17. Play a quarter note followed by a half note and a quarter rest; sing each target before finding it.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[Sources]
John Petrucci, Using Triad Arpeggios to Imply More Complex Chord Qualities: https://www.guitarworld.com/magazine/wild-stringdom-john-petrucci-using-triad-arpeggios-imply-more-complex-chord-qualities
steps.successCriteria: Record eight bars at 60 BPM, alternating fifth and octave targets; every landing is on pitch and on its planned beat. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Hybrid tapping-sweep combos
steps.description:
[What it is]
A tapping-sweep combination connects two established articulations.

[Why it matters]
This is a small integration exercise, not a claim that every Petrucci phrase uses this combination.

[How to practice]
Sweep G14-B13-e12, tap e17, pull back to e12 and descend B13-G14. Write these seven eighth notes followed by an eighth rest; practise the tap-to-pick handoff separately.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

steps.successCriteria: Record eight bars at 50 BPM; all seven events and the rest fit 4/4, the pick returns without a gap and unused strings stay quiet. Use two consecutive clean takes unless the task specifies another count.

steps.title: Fingerboard skipping patterns
steps.description:
[What it is]
Fingerboard skipping patterns apply a skip to more than one location.

[Why it matters]
This develops navigation beyond repeating the same two notes.

[How to practice]
Find A minor triad notes on nonadjacent strings in two positions. Write a four-note pattern in each position, play each for one bar of eighth notes and leave a bar to shift at first.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

steps.title: Syncopated tapping phrasing
steps.description:
[What it is]
Syncopated tapping places a familiar gesture away from the beat.

[Why it matters]
Keep the subdivision steady instead of speeding up to fit the notes.

[How to practice]
In 4/4 use an eighth rest followed by tap12-pull5-hammer8 on high E, then two quarter rests. Repeat this complete four-beat pattern without shortening its rests.

steps.title: Harmonic minor fluency
steps.description:
[What it is]
Harmonic minor raises natural minor degree 7.

[Why it matters]
Its immediate purpose here is hearing the leading tone resolve over a dominant-to-minor cadence, not learning unrelated scale boxes.

[How to practice]
Over E7-Am, play A-B-C-D-E-F-G#-A in one comfortable position. Isolate G#-A at the chord change, then build a two-bar eighth-note phrase. The linked sweep drill is preparation, not a scale test.

steps.title: Melodic minor fluency
steps.description:
[What it is]
Melodic minor provides another minor colour: the jazz form raises degrees 6 and 7 in both directions.

[Why it matters]
Compare its sound directly with harmonic minor rather than treating the names as interchangeable.

[How to practice]
Over an Am drone compare A-B-C-D-E-F-G#-A with A-B-C-D-E-F#-G#-A as eighth notes. Use the latter form in both directions and finish a short phrase on A or C.

steps.title: Phrygian dominant usage
steps.description:
[What it is]
Phrygian dominant is the fifth mode of harmonic minor.

[Why it matters]
Its major third and flat second make it different from ordinary Phrygian; use it in a defined dominant context.

[How to practice]
Over E7-Am use E-F-G#-A-B-C-D-E in eighth notes, first slowly. Build a phrase over E7 that resolves G# to A when Am arrives; compare F against the E bass.

steps.title: Diminished scale fluency
steps.description:
[What it is]
The half-whole diminished scale alternates semitone and tone.

[Why it matters]
Unlike a diminished arpeggio it has eight notes; this step practises one dominant application only.

[How to practice]
Over E7 play E-F-G-G#-A#-B-C#-D as eighth notes, then resolve to A-C-E over Am. Write the interval pattern first. The linked note hunt locates pitches but does not teach this scale.

steps.title: Modal interchange application
steps.description:
[What it is]
Modal interchange borrows a chord from a parallel key while retaining the tonal centre.

[Why it matters]
It gives a theme a contrasting harmonic setting; it is not simply changing scale positions.

[How to practice]
Compose four bars using C-Am-F-Fm, one chord per bar at 60 BPM. Keep a short melody over the first three chords, then change A to Ab over Fm and resolve to G when returning to C.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

steps.title: Diatonic triad stacking
steps.description:
[What it is]
Diatonic triad stacking combines triad tones to suggest a richer harmony.

[Why it matters]
First establish each triad separately so the combined sound is a choice.

[How to practice]
Play G-B-D and E-G-B over a G drone, then the same notes over E. Use quarter notes first and write the combined pitch set; compare the sound of G6 with Em7.

steps.title: Intervallic sequence fluency
steps.description:
[What it is]
Intervallic sequences repeat a relationship rather than merely climbing a scale.

[Why it matters]
Short sequences can connect positions and lead back to a melody.

[How to practice]
In E natural minor play successive diatonic thirds E-G, F#-A, G-B, A-C as eighth notes. Continue for one bar, then answer with a held E or G; mark the target before playing.

[Practice check]

steps.title: Odd-meter groove execution
steps.description:
[What it is]
Odd-meter groove groups unequal numbers of subdivisions without losing the pulse.

[Why it matters]
A small riff is more useful here than a long list of time signatures.

[How to practice]
Clap then play an E5 eighth-note riff in 5/8 grouped 3+2 and 7/8 grouped 2+2+3. Count the groups aloud before adding a melodic ending; keep the eighth-note click constant.

[Practice check]

steps.title: Polyrhythm subdivision control
steps.description:
[What it is]
A polyrhythm layers different equal subdivisions over the same span.

[Why it matters]
Practise 3:2 here; an odd-length motif across a beat is a different concept handled in the next step on displacement.

[How to practice]
Use a six-slot grid across two quarter-note beats: tap one layer on slots 1 and 4, another on 1, 3 and 5. Record the two-hit layer, then play three equally spaced muted notes over it.

[Practice check]

steps.title: Syncopated riffing control
steps.description:
[What it is]
Syncopated riffing makes rests and offbeat entries part of the riff.

[Why it matters]
Palm muting must preserve both the accents and the spaces.

[How to practice]
Write one bar of E5 eighth notes with rests on beat 1 and beat 3, entering on the and of each. Repeat, then add a two-note fill on beat 4 without moving the next entry.

steps.title: Rhythmic displacement phrasing
steps.description:
[What it is]
Rhythmic displacement moves a motif relative to a stable beat.

[Why it matters]
A group of seven sixteenths is not the same as seven equal notes inside one beat.

[How to practice]
Write a four-eighth-note melody. Play it on beat 1, then after an eighth rest in the next bar, completing each bar with rests. Keep the notes and their spacing unchanged; return to beat 1 in bar 3.

steps.title: Motif development techniques
steps.description:
[What it is]
Motif development keeps an identifiable musical idea through changes.

[Why it matters]
Petrucci describes melody as the element that gives instrumental music direction.

[How to practice]
Write a two-bar motif, then three two-bar variations: change rhythm, change register, and alter the ending to fit a new chord. Finish by repeating the original motif.

steps.title: Dynamic contour control
steps.description:
[What it is]
Dynamic contour shapes the intensity of a section, not only individual pick strokes.

[Why it matters]
Use contrasting textures to make a return or climax audible.

[How to practice]
Arrange eight bars: two clean and sparse, two with fuller chords, two with a rising lead, two returning to the quiet theme. Try Cmaj7 x32000 and Aadd9 x02400 with open B and E ringing.

steps.title: Metric modulation awareness
steps.description:
[What it is]
Metric modulation changes the tempo reference through an explicit rhythmic equivalence.

[Why it matters]
Keeping an eighth-note pulse while changing meter is not metric modulation.

[How to practice]
Set quarter note = 60 BPM and play four bars of quarter-note triplets. Treat those triplet attacks as the new quarter pulse at 90 BPM for four bars. Use a programmed tempo change or recorded reference to check the junction.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

steps.title: Emulate Petrucci phrasing
steps.description:
[What it is]
Emulating phrasing means shaping a line through melody, space and articulation.

[Why it matters]
Add expressive control to the techniques already learned rather than filling every beat with notes.

[How to practice]
Write four bars over Em-C-G-D with a rest, an answered motif, a whole-tone bend to a chord tone and a held note with vibrato. Compare each bend with its fretted target before adding vibrato.

[Practice check]

steps.title: Transcribe Petrucci solos
steps.description:
[What it is]
Transcribing solos begins with a bounded phrase and grows into a longer excerpt.

[Why it matters]
Learn pitches and rhythm by ear before checking a transcription; a full solo remains a longer-term extension.

[How to practice]
Choose 10-20 seconds from a Petrucci solo, such as a melodic passage in Out of the Blue. Save the recording version and start/end times. Work in two-second chunks, write pitches, rhythm and articulation, then compare your performance with slowed audio.

[Practice check]

steps.title: Apply Petrucci licks
steps.description:
[What it is]
Applying a lick adapts its musical function instead of inserting it unchanged.

[Why it matters]
Use the previous transcription as material and keep its recognizable contour.

[How to practice]
Choose one short motif from your transcription. Write a two-bar response over its original harmony, then change the ending for a different chord and shift its starting beat. Combine source motif and responses into eight bars.

steps.title: Compose Petrucci-style themes
steps.description:
[What it is]
Composing a theme organizes technique around a musical identity.

[Why it matters]
An original short form demonstrates transfer beyond copying a recording.

[How to practice]
Write a two-bar theme and build a 16-bar A-B-A arrangement: four bars of theme, eight of contrasting riff/lead material, four returning to the theme. Include one odd-meter passage, one clean texture and one short technical phrase resolving to a chord tone.

steps.title: Perform Dream Theater parts
steps.description:
[What it is]
Performing Dream Theater parts means reproducing a defined section in its arrangement.

[Why it matters]
A manageable excerpt lets you assess rhythm, tone and transitions without demanding an entire catalogue.

[How to practice]
Choose 30-60 seconds of a Dream Theater recording containing a rhythm part and a transition, for example from On the Backs of Angels. Note the exact release, time range and tuning; use a verified transcription or learn it by ear. Rehearse the transition separately, then join the section against slowed playback.

steps.title: High-gain articulation control
steps.description:
[What it is]
High-gain articulation preserves the note and the pause through distortion.

[Why it matters]
This final check applies earlier muting to the actual riff and solo you will perform.

[How to practice]
Use four bars from your selected rhythm part and four from your solo excerpt. Record with lower gain and performance gain at the same playback speed; adjust palm/fretting-hand muting and gain so stops remain audible. Feedback and pinch harmonics are only needed if the selected part uses them.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

steps.title: Live solo arrangement
steps.description:
[What it is]
Live solo arrangement makes the learned excerpt reliable in a performance context.

[Why it matters]
Preserve its anchor points while planning a simpler recovery route and an intentional ending.

[How to practice]
Arrange 30-60 seconds around your transcribed solo phrase: mark entry, climax and resolution, add one variation and list effect changes. Rehearse against a backing track; in a separate practice take leave one phrase out deliberately and rejoin at the next marked anchor.

[Practice check]
Use the completion task below as a self-check. Tempos and repetitions are curriculum targets, not claims about Petrucci's own practice. Start slower when needed; BPM means quarter notes unless another pulse is stated.

[What you can do now]
Play bounded Petrucci/Dream Theater excerpts at documented learning tempos, control picking and legato, use arpeggios over stated harmony, keep odd-meter riffs in time, and arrange an original theme with expressive phrasing. Full album-tempo solos remain a further goal.
